verdict.reasoning: Patient states diarrhea has been present for about three days and is going to the toilet around 5–6 times per day with watery, loose stools: "I've been having, uh, diarrhoea, for like, let's say past three days" and "around, five to six times a day" and "it's definitely, definitely watery, uh, loose stools".

Patient reports diarrhea started with vomiting a couple of times which then resolved: "it started with vomiting, so I vomited a couple of times. Uh, but then, that went away, and, uh, yeah it's just diarrhoea now."

Stools are watery: "it's definitely, definitely watery, uh, loose stools"; no blood: "Any blood in your stools?" "No, not that I could see"; no abdominal pain: "with the diarrhea have you noticed any other symptoms, like tummy pain?" "Uh, not, not really, no"; no headache or muscle pains: "Any headaches or muscle pains?" "Not, not really, no."

Patient feels dehydrated and weak with little oral intake and a brief early temperature: "I feel very dehydrated" and describes trying to drink but still feeling dehydrated; minimal solids: "have you managed to eat anything, solids?" "Uh, not much, not much"; weakness: "I feel very weak though"; brief fever: "probably at, at the beginning I was feeling I had a bit of temperature, but now I feel, I feel kind of fine."
Patient explicitly reports asthma: "so I, I do suffer of asthma."

Patient uses an inhaler infrequently and doctor confirms it is the blue inhaler (a short-acting beta-agonist): "I do have my inhalers... I use infrequently" and doctor: "Is that the blue inhaler?" Patient: "Yes it is, yeah."
Patient denies medication allergies: "Do you have any allergies to medications?" "Um, not that I know of."
Patient reports father had high blood pressure and died of bowel cancer: "my father has, high uh, well used to have high blood pressure. He actually... died, of, bowel cancer, like ten years ago."
Mother’s type 2 diabetes is stated: "she has diabetes" and when asked type: "Uh, it's type two."
Patient confirms living alone and occupation: "Who lives at home with you?" "Ohh I, I live alone." and "What's your employment?" "I'm a software engineer."
He has been off work three days and does not smoke: "these last three days I've been feeling, really unwell, so I couldn't work" and "I don't smoke."
Social alcohol use stated: "not really, I drink infrequently, like socially let's say."

Doctor diagnoses gastroenteritis but does not specify viral: "I think you're probably suffering from what we call gastroenteritis"; describing it as an infection and tummy bug, but the word "viral" is never used, so labeling it as acute viral gastroenteritis adds etiology not in transcript.

Patient feels dehydrated and has frequent watery diarrhea with poor intake, which clinically indicates risk of mild dehydration: "I feel very dehydrated" and diarrhea 5–6 times/day with minimal solids. This is a direct clinical inference.

Asthma is mentioned but there is no explicit statement or discussion of current control or stability; "I do have my inhalers... I use infrequently" suggests but does not clearly document an assessment that asthma is stable.

Doctor advises oral rehydration solution and increased fluids: "you can drink plenty of fluids" and "you can get things from the pharmacy, which is called Dioralyte, which can help replenish any uh minerals and vitamins you may have lost... it's a type of fluid replacement drink."
Paracetamol advice is explicit: "you can take some Paracetamol if you're feeling feverish and weak."

Doctor advises time off and return criteria: "I would probably advise you to continue taking time off work for next day or two" and "normally you have to be diarrhea-free for about twenty four to forty eight hours, before you return back to work."

Follow-up if not improved within about a week is clearly stated: "let's see how the next few days go. And if you're still not better next week, I want you to come back and see me." This aligns with returning if no improvement within 7 days; worsening is implied by need to come back if not better.
There is no explicit instruction to continue using the blue inhaler as needed; asthma medication is only elicited in history, without a plan statement about inhaler use.
